lead: A half-wave dipole is a straight wire half a wavelength long, fed at its centre. At that length the wire resonates: the current stands as a cosine, largest at the feed and zero at the tips, and the input resistance is about 73 Ω. It is the reference antenna of radio. The quarter-wave monopole is half of it on a ground plane, and the folded dipole is two of them joined at the ends.
prereq: You need: radiation resistance and directivity (radiation resistance and efficiency) and the Hertzian dipole field.

blocks.text: The tips of the wire are open circuits, so the current must be zero there. Fed at the centre, a thin wire of total length l = λ/2 carries a standing wave of current
I(z) = I₀ cos(βz), −λ/4 ≤ z ≤ λ/4. I₀ is the peak current at the centre in A; z is the distance from the centre in m; β = 2π/λ
The current is a cosine half-arch, fuller than the triangular current of a short dipole, so the half-wave dipole radiates far more for the same feed current.

An exactly half-wave thin dipole has input impedance Zin = 73 + j42.5 Ω. The 73 Ω is radiation resistance; the +j42.5 Ω is inductive reactance from stored near-field energy. Shortening the wire slightly makes it capacitive, and at about 0.47λ to 0.48λ (thicker wire needs more shortening) the reactance cancels and the input is close to a pure resistance near 70 Ω: a good match to 75 Ω coaxial cable.

sections.h3: Far field, directivity and radiation resistance

blocks.text: Adding the fields of Hertzian elements carrying I(z), each with its own phase, gives the far field
Eθ = j 60 I₀ e−jβr cos((π/2) cos θ) / (r sin θ). Eθ in V/m, I₀ in A, r in m; Hφ = Eθ/η
Broadside the magnitude is simply |E| = 60 I₀/r. The pattern is a doughnut slightly slimmer than the short dipole’s.
Integrating the power gives P<sub>rad</sub> = ½ I₀² × 73.1 W, so R<sub>r</sub> = 73 Ω at the feed. A link budget uses the gain, 2.15 dBi; the 73 Ω is what the feed line must match.

sections.h3: Quarter-wave monopole over a ground plane

blocks.text: Stand one half of the dipole, λ/4 long, on a large conducting sheet and feed it against the sheet. By image theory a perfect, infinite ground plane acts as a mirror: wire plus image is the half-wave dipole. Above the plane the fields are the dipole’s; below it there is none.

items: Impedance: the same current radiates only the upper half of the dipole’s power, so Z<sub>in</sub> = ½(73 + j42.5) = 36.5 + j21.25 Ω, close to 50 Ω coaxial cable once trimmed.
Directivity: that half power fills only half the space, so D = 2 × 1.64 = 3.28, that is 5.16 dBi. The pattern is the top half of the doughnut.
Size: λ/4 is half the dipole’s length: 0.75 m at 100 MHz, 3.1 cm at 2.4 GHz.

blocks.text: Real ground planes are finite (mast radials, a car roof, a phone’s circuit board), so the impedance and gain move away from these ideals.

Bend a wire one wavelength long into a narrow loop λ/2 long, its two parallel sides a small distance s ≪ λ apart and joined at both ends, and feed one side at its centre. This is the folded dipole. On the antenna mode both sides carry equal currents in the same direction, so for the same feed current I the radiating current is 2I and the field is doubled. Power goes as field squared, so the same feed current delivers four times the power: Rin = 4 × 73 = 292 Ω, usually called 300 Ω. With N equal parallel wires the step-up is N².
That matches 300 Ω twin-lead, which is why TV Yagis use a folded driven element; the fatter effective conductor also widens the bandwidth.

A dipole is balanced: its two arms are symmetric about ground. Coaxial cable is unbalanced: its outer conductor is at ground. Connected directly, current flows on the outside of the shield and skews the pattern. A balun (balanced to unbalanced) sits between them: a transformer, a λ/4 sleeve, or a λ/2 loop of coax, which also steps impedance 4 : 1.

figure.caption: Current along the worked examples’ 100 MHz antennas. On the 1.41 m dipole it is a cosine, largest at the feed and zero at the tips (a short dipole’s falls in a straight line); the 0.75 m monopole carries the top half, and the ground plane supplies the mirror image.

spec.aria: Left: a vertical dipole 1.41 metres long with its cosine current envelope, maximum at the centre feed, zero at the tips, and a dashed triangle for a short dipole; about 73 ohms, directivity 1.64. Right: a quarter-wave monopole 0.75 metres tall on a ground plane with a dashed image below; 36.5 ohms, directivity 3.28.

examples.question: A half-wave dipole for 100 MHz is cut to 0.47λ and carries a feed current of 1 A peak. Find its length, the radiated power, the broadside field and power density at 1 km, and check the power density with the directivity.
steps: Check: S = D P<sub>rad</sub>/(4πr²) = 1.64 × 36.5/(4π × 10⁶) = 4.76 × 10⁻⁶ W/m². The two agree; the 0.2 % gap is only because 73 Ω and 1.64 are rounded.
examples.answer: l = 1.41 m; P<sub>rad</sub> = 36.5 W; |E| = 60 mV/m and S = 4.77 µW/m² at 1 km broadside.

examples.question: A quarter-wave monopole on a car roof works at 100 MHz and is fed with the same 36.5 W as the dipole above. Taking the roof as a perfect ground plane, find its length, its feed current, and its field at 1 km along the ground. Compare with the dipole.
steps: Feed current: P = ½ I₀² × 36.5, so I₀² = 2 × 36.5/36.5 = 2 and I₀ = 1.414 A.
Above the plane the field is that of a dipole carrying the same current: |E| = 60 I₀/r = 60 × 1.414/1000 = 0.0849 V/m = 84.9 mV/m.
Compared with the dipole: 84.9/60 = 1.414 in field, 2 in power, that is 3.01 dB more, because the same power fills half the space.
examples.answer: l = 0.75 m; I₀ = 1.414 A; |E| = 84.9 mV/m at 1 km, 3 dB above the dipole for the same power.

traps: Giving a half-wave dipole D = 1.5. That is the short dipole; the half-wave value is 1.64 (2.15 dBi).
Writing Z<sub>in</sub> = 73 Ω for an exact λ/2 dipole. It is 73 + j42.5 Ω; shortening to about 0.47λ to 0.48λ removes the reactance.
Giving the quarter-wave monopole 73 Ω or 2.15 dBi. It is 36.5 Ω and 5.16 dBi over a perfect ground plane.
Saying the folded dipole has twice the resistance. Field doubles, power quadruples: 4 × 73 = 292 Ω.
Using P = I₀²R with a peak current. For a sinusoid it is ½ I₀² R.

quiz.q: State the input impedance of an exact half-wave dipole and why practical dipoles are cut shorter.
quiz.a: 73 + j42.5 Ω. Cutting to about 0.47λ to 0.48λ adds capacitive reactance that cancels the +j42.5 Ω, leaving a nearly pure resistance.

quiz.q: Why is the current zero at the tips of a dipole?
quiz.a: The tips are open ends: charge cannot flow beyond them, so the standing wave has a current null at each tip and its maximum at the centre.

quiz.q: A quarter-wave monopole works at 300 MHz over a large ground plane. Find its length and input resistance.
quiz.a: λ = 1 m, length = 0.25 m, R<sub>in</sub> = ½ × 73 = 36.5 Ω.

quiz.q: A half-wave dipole carries a feed current of 2 A peak. Find the radiated power and the broadside field at 5 km.
Why does the quarter-wave monopole have twice the directivity of the half-wave dipole?
quiz.a: The ground plane removes all radiation below it, so the same power is concentrated into half the space: D = 3.28 instead of 1.64 (5.16 against 2.15 dBi).

quiz.q: Show numerically why a folded dipole suits 300 Ω twin-lead better than a plain dipole.
quiz.a: Folded: Γ = (292 − 300)/(292 + 300) = −0.0135, VSWR 1.03, return loss 37.4 dB. Plain: Γ = (73 − 300)/(73 + 300) = −0.609, VSWR 4.11, return loss 4.3 dB, so 37 % of the power is reflected.

quiz.q: A quarter-wave monopole on a small metal box measures well above 36.5 Ω. Suggest two causes.
quiz.a: A small plane makes a poor image, so the structure behaves partly like a full dipole and the resistance moves up towards 73 Ω. A lossy plane or poor bonding adds loss resistance in series. Current on the outside of the feed coax also shifts the reading.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modules use a printed dipole or monopole etched on the board, often meandered to fit; real dipole impedance depends on wire radius and is computed by induced-EMF or moment methods. Search next for “printed dipole” and “induced EMF method”.
